solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Vain display of power by head of Ofsted and Gove, perhaps

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: P is the standard abbreviation for power
the first letter of the inspectorate's name
Michael Gove is an example of a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A jibe at a former Education Secretary and the schools inspectorate for showing off their authority.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofsted is England's schools inspectorate and Michael Gove a former Education Secretary, so the surface reads as political satire; 'by' just places the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomp is ceremonial splendour, often with the suggestion of empty, self-important show.

clue.text: It could be important on holiday to agree to drink

definitions.text: It could be important on holiday

blocks.note: to pass a motion or bill is to approve it
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Someone on holiday thinks it may matter to accept an offered drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic hint: the document you must carry abroad matters greatly when travelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is the travel document you cannot do without when going abroad, so it matters on a foreign holiday.

clue.text: Something to sing about finally – champagne all round

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the preceding word only
all round says the drink's name wraps itself around what precedes it

blocks.note: the closing letter of this word
Moët is a famous champagne house

explanation.surface: A celebration: at last there is something worth singing about, so champagne for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stops at 'sing': 'about' belongs to the wordplay, though the surface makes 'something to sing about' one phrase. MOET goes round T.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a short choral composition, usually sacred, written to be sung.

clue.text: Smarmy count peculiar about university in front of American

indicators.note: something peculiar is out of the ordinary, so the letters come out of their usual order
about means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go around the next piece
in front of says this assembled group comes before the final piece

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
U is the usual abbreviation for university
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A description of an oily, peculiar aristocrat at a university, followed by an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'count' looks like a nobleman described as smarmy, but it is the fodder; the university letter goes inside the rearranged word before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Unctuous literally means oily, and figuratively describes an ingratiating, excessively flattering manner, which is what smarmy means.

clue.text: Throw up on lens, drunk with no energy

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order
with no says the following item is left out of the letters

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A drunk vomits on someone's camera lens and is left with no energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw up' looks like one phrase meaning vomit, but the definition is 'Throw' alone, in its sense of disconcert.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw someone is to confuse or disconcert them, just as nonplus means to bewilder so they do not know how to react.

clue.text: Flat broke so timid with new loan

indicators.note: broke is the past of break, so the letters are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, taken as written
anagram fodder, taken as written
anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy person, flat broke, takes out a fresh loan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat broke' reads as one phrase for penniless, but 'Flat' is the definition and 'broke' signals the rearrangement. 'with' joins the pieces of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something two-dimensional has length and breadth but no depth, so it is flat; figuratively it means shallow.

clue.text: Aida possibly moving into management

indicators.note: moving says the following word's letters shift position

blocks.note: Verdi's Aida is an example of an opera
the fodder word rearranged

explanation.surface: Verdi's opera Aida is being taken over by new management.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving into' reads as one phrase, but 'into' is the fodder for the rearrangement signalled by 'moving'.
explanation.definitionFit: The operation of a business is its running or management, as in being responsible for day-to-day operations.

clue.text: Plant also unknown by Academy

blocks.note: so can mean also, as in 'so do I'
algebra uses x, y and z for unknown quantities
A is a standard abbreviation for Academy

explanation.surface: A plant of unknown origin has also been found beside an academy.
explanation.definitionFit: Soya is the soybean plant, a legume grown for its protein-rich beans and oil.

clue.text: Show-off aunt sang – unfortunately not a shortened piece

indicators.note: something that has gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the letters end up disordered
not says the following item must be taken away from the letters

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
one of these letters is removed

explanation.surface: An attention-seeking aunt sang, and sadly it was not a short performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' is slang for a gun, and a shortened one is a gun whose barrel has been cut down.
explanation.definitionFit: A sawn-off shotgun has its barrel cut short, and piece is criminal slang for a firearm.

clue.text: Signs of protest from Italian caught in acts of wickedness

indicators.note: caught in says one thing is trapped inside another

blocks.note: It is Italian vermouth, as in gin and It
sins are wicked acts

explanation.surface: Protests break out after an Italian is caught doing wicked things.
explanation.walkthrough: Italian vermouth is known in Britain as It, as in the cocktail gin and It.
explanation.definitionFit: Sit-ins are protests in which people occupy a place and refuse to leave, so they are demonstrations of dissent.

clue.text: Bottom perhaps to undergo an examination with medication you ordered? Not I!

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
Not I says that letter must be removed before rearranging

blocks.note: to sit an exam is to take it
the anagram fodder, taken as written
this letter is struck out of the fodder

explanation.surface: A nervous patient asks whether they must have an exam and medication, insisting it is not for them.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom was a 1990s BBC sitcom starring Rik Mayall and Ade Edmondson; the word looks like an anatomical hint that fits the medical surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottom is an example of a sitcom, a comedy series built around recurring characters in a fixed setting.

clue.text: Powerful drug late in working

indicators.note: working suggests being worked on and reshaped, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: pot is slang for cannabis
the fodder rearranged

explanation.surface: A strong drug kicks in late once it starts working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Powerful drug' looks like the definition with a drug to find, but 'Powerful' alone is the definition, in a rare old sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Potential in an older sense means potent or mighty, sharing a Latin root with potent and power.

clue.text: One leads in mosque, aiding Muslims

definitions.text: One leads in mosque, aiding Muslims

indicators.note: leads means the front runners, so only the opening letter of each following word counts

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
the first letters of mosque, aiding and Muslims; 'in' is not counted

explanation.surface: A description of the person who leads worship in a mosque, helping the faithful.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay; 'in' joins the parts and gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An imam is the prayer leader of a mosque, guiding the congregation in worship.

clue.text: Rent's getting high in instances of daylight robbery

indicators.note: getting means taking in, so one piece receives the other inside it

blocks.note: rents are tears in fabric, the same as rips
food that is high has started to go off

explanation.surface: Rising rents are described as daylight robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid to a landlord; here it is a tear. Meat that is high is going bad, i.e. off.
explanation.definitionFit: A rip-off is a gross overcharge, and daylight robbery is the British idiom for being blatantly overcharged.

clue.text: Plant most of the grass on the trail of earth, perhaps

indicators.note: most of means all but a bit, so the final letter is dropped
on the trail of means following behind, so this piece comes after the other

blocks.note: Earth is an example of a planet
a reed is a tall grass

explanation.surface: Instructions to sow grass along a path through the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'earth' looks like soil to go with the gardening surface, but it is the planet; the grass piece follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: The plane is a broad-leaved tree, often seen lining London streets, so it is a kind of plant.

clue.text: Dramatic changes since beginning of coalition

indicators.note: changes says the following word's letters are altered in order
the beginning of a word is its opening letter only

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written
the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: A political commentator notes dramatic changes since a coalition government began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dramatic changes' reads as one phrase, but 'Dramatic' is the definition and 'changes' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenic can mean relating to the stage or theatrical scenery, hence theatrical or dramatic.

clue.text: In the main it is glass

blocks.note: first meaning: a sailing ship, found out on the main, the open sea
second meaning: a tall glass for sherry or beer

explanation.surface: Someone asserts that, on the whole, the thing in question is glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' looks like 'mostly', but the main is the open sea, where a sailing ship is found.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a fore-and-aft rigged sailing vessel and a large drinking glass for sherry or beer.

clue.text: Blackcurrant flavouring finally replaced with a kind of cinnamon

indicators.note: finally replaced says the last letter is swapped out for what follows

blocks.note: cassis is a blackcurrant liqueur or syrup
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe swaps its blackcurrant flavouring at the last moment for a type of cinnamon.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' is the replacement letter and also opens the surface's 'a kind of cinnamon', so the definition starts at 'kind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassia is the bark of a related tree sold as Chinese cinnamon, a coarser kind of the spice.

clue.text: A non-drinker maintains the chap is a non-believer

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so one piece holds the other inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
TT stands for teetotal
the chap is 'he', followed by 'is' as written

explanation.surface: Someone who avoids alcohol insists that a certain man has no religious faith.
explanation.walkthrough: TT, short for teetotal, holds HE IS, and A goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheist rejects belief in any god, so is a non-believer in the religious sense.

clue.text: Cheeky thing to almost steal poison

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: arse is British slang for the bottom, made of two cheeks
nick is British slang for steal

explanation.surface: A cheeky person is about to steal some poison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' suggests impudence; here the thing with cheeks is the backside, in British slang the arse. To nick is to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is a chemical element whose compounds are notoriously toxic, long used as a poison.

clue.text: Song the man played in Perpignan – the Marseillaise?

indicators.note: played suggests being toyed with, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A man plays a song in the French city of Perpignan; was it the Marseillaise?
explanation.walkthrough: The Marseillaise, France's national song, is an example, hence the question mark. As a bonus the answer also sits hidden in 'PerpignAN THE Marseillaise'.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthem is a rousing song of praise or loyalty, and the Marseillaise is France's national one.

clue.text: Throw out offensive tomato sandwiches

indicators.note: to sandwich is to hold between, so the words around hold the letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone rejects sandwiches made with an unpleasant tomato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like a noun for lunch; it is a verb saying the two words contain the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To veto a proposal is to reject it outright, which is to throw it out.

clue.text: Stolen jacket, maybe – a tricky case

blocks.note: hot is slang for stolen goods
a jacket potato is one baked in its skin

explanation.surface: A detective investigates a stolen jacket and finds it a difficult case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jacket' looks like clothing, but a jacket potato is a British baked potato; hot means stolen, as in hot goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot potato is an awkward, controversial issue that people would rather not handle.

clue.text: Tie it up on bed

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: it means sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: An instruction to tie something to a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' meaning sex appeal (SA) is a crossword convention; read upwards it sits on top of COT.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a wide cravat-style necktie, named after the Berkshire racecourse.

clue.text: Bishop abandoned jugs on east section of church

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so that letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
jugs and baps are both British slang for breasts
E is short for east

explanation.surface: A bishop leaves some jugs on the east side of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: Baps are bread rolls, and like jugs are British slang for breasts; losing the B for bishop leaves APS.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the semicircular recess at the end of a church, usually at the east end behind the altar.

clue.text: Dad in Paris prepared for cleaning bird

indicators.note: prepared means made ready by working on, so the letters are reshaped

blocks.note: père is French for father
the fodder, rearranged

explanation.surface: A French father gets ready to do the cleaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The peregrine falcon is a bird of prey famous as the fastest diving creature on earth.

clue.text: Type of ring European attached to bird softly, out of compassion

indicators.note: out of means taken away from, so that letter leaves the word that follows

blocks.note: E is short for European
a tern is a seabird
p is the musical marking piano, softly
pity is compassion

explanation.surface: A European fond of a bird gives it a ring out of kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: P for softly is the musical marking piano, removed from PITY.
explanation.definitionFit: An eternity ring is a band set all round with gems, symbolising everlasting love.

clue.text: Move the can

blocks.note: first meaning: to budge or start moving
second meaning: slang for prison

explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a tin to be shifted, but both the can and stir are slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir means to move slightly, and it is also slang for jail, just like the can.
